letters.title: From [?]   [?]
letters.summary: Hybrid fish.

letters.title: From [?]   [?]
letters.summary: "but most of them [verily?] Christened by myself they may be indulged with a"

letters.title: From [?]   [?]
letters.summary: [Fragmentary strip.] Discusses pigeons, Australia, Regents Park.

letters.title: To ?   [?]
letters.summary: Asks correspondent if he would prefer the President’s signature alone or with those of other scientific men.

letters.title: To ?   [?]
letters.summary: Can the correspondent get some pamphlets written by Dr [Max?] Stengel.

letters.title: To ?   [?]
letters.summary: [Signature cut from a letter; the reverse contains the words "you must … that I know nothing of your private".]

letters.title: To ? [a librarian]   [13? September 1854]
letters.summary: Will return all but two volumes; requests four titles, including Pepys’sDiaries, but not the first volume.

letters.title: From Mary Congreve27 October [1821]
letters.summary: Writes about London plays; wishes CD had been of the party.

letters.title: To Dear Friend   1 January 1822
letters.summary: Erasmus Alvey Darwin has rheumatism; his sisters complain of his bad temper but CD thinks him very good tempered. CD has received a new cabinet. [This is the first of six entries written in a "Memorandum book" comprising four sheets folded into a gather and sewn together in book form. The entries are in the style of letters addressed to an unnamed friend and are dated between 1 and 12 January 1822, shortly before CD’s thirteenth birthday. As they were written straight into the memorandum book, it is clear that they were never sent through the post, but were either to an imaginary recipient, or intended to be read by someone in the household, possibly CD’s youngest sister, Emily Catherine Darwin (Catherine).]

letters.title: To Dear Friend   2 January 1822
letters.summary: Erasmus Alvey Darwin is good tempered and their sisters have "not abused at all". Hopes the recipient will help "in looking out and washing the fossils out of the plate closet".

letters.title: To Dear Friend   3 January 1822
letters.summary: "Monseur Beodoes" is inquisitive and impertinent; Mr Bayly "was formerly adevlishboor". Asks who his sisters have been talking about.

letters.title: To Dear Friend   4 January 1822
letters.summary: Likes Mariane who is very good to Miss Jones; CD bought cakes in town while Mariane visited Miss Jones; he was embarrassed to be shown into her bedroom when he returned. Miss Clare has had an accident.

letters.title: To Dear Friend   4 January 1822
letters.summary: Caroline disapproves of his not washing.

letters.title: To Dear Friend   12 January 1822
letters.summary: Was joined by Colonel Burgh Leighton when walking in the quarry. Plans to make caves next summer to store "warlike instruments" and "relicks". Sketches a design for a signalling device. May go with his father to visit the Earl of Powys at Walcot; visited Mrs and Miss Reynolds and William Pemberton Cludde.

letters.title: From Erasmus Alvey Darwin   25 [October 1822]
letters.summary: Has found a shop with supplies of chemical equipment, and a mineral collector.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   14 November 1822
letters.summary:
EAD wants changes made and shelves built to improve the laboratory at the Mount [Darwin residence]; sends drawings and will bring chemical instruments, a book, and his record of experiments done in his chemistry course.

He has now been matriculated.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   8 December 1822
letters.summary: Suggestions for laboratory equipment. Will buy some mineral specimens. Describes experiments he has seen.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   5 [March 1823]
letters.summary: More suggestions for the laboratory, including some experiments.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   18 May 1823
letters.summary: Discusses plans for CD to visit Cambridge.

letters.title: From Emily Catherine Darwin  [c.June 1823]
letters.summary:
Writes, while visiting the Wedgwoods at Maer and Parkfields, to thank CD for his "entertaining letter".

She misses him and the laboratory.

Asks "how Mineralogy, Botany, Chemistry and Entomology go on".

letters.title: From John Wood Warter23 December 1824
letters.summary:
Warns CD against idleness.

Suggests readings in Xenophon and Horace.

Quotes Oliver Goldsmith to correct CD’s pronunciation of "sloth".

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin [10 January 1825]
letters.summary:
Saw a mineral salesman, but he had nothing CD does not already have.

EAD has a piece of petrified sponge and some curious coal that John Price pulled out of his fire.

Griffith’sAnimal kingdom[Georges Cuvier,The animal kingdom … with additional descriptions of speciesby Edward Griffith (1827–35)] just being published. He is sure CD would like it.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin [17 January 1825]
letters.summary:
Proposes a dry place for the apparatus for their laboratory and draws a plan for CD’s criticism.

Price has found black sediment in his tea, which was attracted to a magnet.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin [24 January 1825]
letters.summary:
Asks CD to do an experiment for him.

Has found a curious stone in his fire.

Price’s iron in tea measured 13 per cent.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [1 February 1825]
letters.summary: Tells CD a bill is all right. Hopes his father will pay it and a wine merchant’s bill as well.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [24 February 1825]
letters.summary: EAD thinks it a pity if CD does not go to Cambridge, but it will be very pleasant for them to be together at Edinburgh, where they should go as soon as possible and read. EAD is getting "case-hardened" in anatomy.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin[8 March 1825]
letters.summary: Asks CD to send him some books on physiology and natural history from the family library.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [June 1825]
letters.summary:
Asks CD whether he is making any plans for Edinburgh.

Will be home in three weeks.

letters.title: To Robert Waring Darwin   [23 October 1825]
letters.summary: First days in Edinburgh.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   [26 October 1825]
letters.summary:
Shrewsbury news.

Glad he likes Edinburgh.

They have been going to plays performed by a travelling company he knows.

letters.title: From Catherine & Susan Darwin   4 December [1825]
letters.summary: Family news.

letters.title: From Caroline & Susan Darwin   2 [January 1826]
letters.summary: A ball and two concerts at Shrewsbury; guests at the Darwins’: Mr and Mrs Mathew, three Mr Clives, Emma Wedgwood.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   6 January 1826
letters.summary: CD comments on lectures and lecturers at Edinburgh.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   15 January [1826]
letters.summary: Family news. Visits to the Owens at Woodhouse and the Parkers at Overton.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   29 January [1826]
letters.summary:
Sends thanks to all for their letters.

News of dining and theatre at Edinburgh.

CD will learn to stuff birds from "a blackamoor".

letters.title: From Marianne Parker   [23 February 1826]
letters.summary: Spark has died. Other family news.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   [27 February 1826]
letters.summary:
Theatre at Shrewsbury.

Spark’s death.

Harry [Henry Allen] Wedgwood will make the circuit for the first time at the forthcoming assizes.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [9 March 1826]
letters.summary: Describes his trip by canal to Glasgow, and sightseeing there.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [9 March 1826]
letters.summary: Found his vessel delayed. Spent an hour or so at the Hunterian Museum, "well worth going to".

letters.title: From Marianne Parker   [c.13 March 1826]
letters.summary: Further particulars of Spark’s death.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   [22 March 1826]
letters.summary: Tells of gay times with guests.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   [27 March 1826]
letters.summary:
Writes of Papa’s disapproval of CD’s practice of picking and choosing only lectures he likes to attend and of his early return home.

News of Erasmus, who is visiting sick poor people in the neighbourhood. Other Shrewsbury news.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   8 April [1826]
letters.summary:
CD is studying the Bible, likes the gospels best.

Glad he stayed for T. C. Hope’s lectures on electricity.

Is running short of funds.

letters.title: From Catherine & Caroline Darwin   11 April [1826]
letters.summary: Family and Shrewsbury news. Visits of relatives and friends.

letters.title: From John Price   [July 1826]
letters.summary: Tells CD he is recovering from the illness with which he was afflicted when CD visited.

letters.title: From James Farley Turner   [28 July 1826]
letters.summary: Is coming to Shrewsbury. Finds little to do but hunt rabbits. Has heard from Nathan Hubbersty and Frederick Watkins.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   [29 September 1826]
letters.summary: Describes the lectures at medical school in London.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin   10 October [1826]
letters.summary: Medical studies in London. Compares lectures and students at London and Edinburgh. Comments on the cost of dissection.

letters.title: From Sarah Harriet Owen   31 [December 1827]
letters.deprecated: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.sender: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.summary: They have been having a very gay time. Tells of "Redcoats & Shootables" and several mutual friends.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [January 1828]
letters.summary:
Surprised to hear from Sarah [Owen] that CD has decided to become a D.D., not an M.D.

She has been to a ball or a party almost every night.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [late January 1828]
letters.summary:
Tells him the Woodhouse family will set forth for return home.

Reports on activities in Brighton.

letters.title: From Sarah Owen   18 February [1828]
letters.deprecated: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.sender: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.summary:
Writes of the last part of their lively stay at Brighton and three days in London.

None of CD’s sisters can come to enliven the "truly awful" tranquillity at the Forest [Woodhouse].

letters.title: From Fanny Owen    [9 March 1828]
letters.summary:
Went recently to Tommy Hunt’s festivities before Lloyd Kenyon joined his regiment.

Hopes Caroline and Catherine Darwin will visit in a week.

letters.title: From Sarah Owen    30 March [1828]
letters.deprecated: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.sender: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.summary: Caroline and Catherine Darwin were at the Forest a few days last week and Susan Darwin comes the next day. Mentions other relatives, friends, and acquaintances.

letters.title: To William Darwin Fox   12 [June 1828]
letters.summary: Account of insects he has collected, with figures drawn by sister.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [30 June 1828]
letters.summary: Mainly concerned with entomological specimens CD has recently captured. Three figures of beetles are included.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [July? 1828]
letters.summary: Is eager to know all that goes on at the Forest [Woodhouse], Bliss Castle [Maer], and Darwin Hall [The Mount].

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [29 July 1828]
letters.summary:
CD on a reading party at Barmouth, Wales;

difficulty with mathematics.

Reports on his entomological collecting.

letters.title: To Charles Thomas Whitley    [10 August 1828]
letters.summary: His idle life and the pleasures of Barmouth: "my reading [in mathematics] is a failure"; "Beettle hunting … is my proper sphere".

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [19 August 1828]
letters.summary:
Accepts invitation to a Music Meeting at Osmaston, Derbyshire.

Entomological news and queries.

Has taken up angling.

letters.title: To John Maurice Herbert    [13 September 1828]
letters.summary:
Asks JMH to collect some insects at Barmouth.

Reports on his shooting luck.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [October 1828]
letters.summary:
Sends some stuffed birds for "Osmaston Museum" and some insects.

Home having cloyed, plans to go to Woodhouse to visit the Owens and the black-eyed houris [Sarah and Fanny] there.

letters.title: To the Darwin Family   3 October 1828
letters.summary: [Caroline Darwin on behalf of CD] submits a petition to Darwin family for £20 to purchase a new double-barrelled gun, CD’s present one having become dangerous.

letters.title: To J. M. Herbert    [3 October 1828]
letters.summary:
CD obliged for JMH’s labours in "the science". He reports having spent a pleasant month. Entomological pursuits succeeded.

Looks forward to receiving beetles and butterflies from JMH when he passes through Shrewsbury.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen    [26 October 1828]
letters.summary:
Woodhouse news, including going to a play.

She has been spending much time painting.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [29 October 1828]
letters.summary: Has met Frederick William Hope, the entomologist; relates F. W. Hope’s praise of CD’s collection and his generous offer of assistance.

letters.title: To E. A. Darwin    21 December 1828
letters.summary:
Has found nice rooms in [Christ’s] College, which he has furnished with some very good prints. Lives almost entirely with W. D. Fox and entomology.

News of John Price, B. H. Kennedy, and Charles Whitley. Fanny Owen is as charming as ever.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [24 December 1828]
letters.summary:
CD is collecting entomological specimens;

extols the charms of Fanny Owen.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [7 January 1829]
letters.summary:
Entomological news, his poor success in collecting, observation of chrysalis.

Commiserates with WDF in his dismal pre-examination state.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [25–9 January 1829]
letters.summary:
Congratulates WDF on finishing at Cambridge; he regards his place as a very good one, and comments on how others did.

Father much pleased by gift of a swan.

Adds some entomological news.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [26 February 1829]
letters.summary:
Entomological visits with F. W. Hope and J. F. Stephens in London. News of insects taken and birds shot.

Has been advised by his tutor to defer the "Little Go". Sends news of Cambridge friends.

letters.title: From John Coldstream   28 February 1829
letters.summary:
News of his activities in recent months, of mutual Edinburgh acquaintances, and the Plinian Society.

JC has given up natural history for a time to prepare himself better for medical practice.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [15 March 1829]
letters.summary:
His routine days at Cambridge.

Entomology stopped for the present.

His reading, gambling, and parties. News of Cambridge friends.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    1 April [1829]
letters.summary:
Eager to hear how WDF and his family get on.

Entomology goes poorly. Harbour has given C. C. Babington first pick of the beetles, and CD has stopped buying from him.

Fire at Linton.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [10 April 1829]
letters.summary:
Has been in "a perfect and absolute state of idleness", riding and walking in the morning, gambling at Van John [vingt-et-un] in the evening.

"Little Go" has been unusually strict.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [12 April 1829]
letters.summary: CD writes with much sympathy for WDF, whose sister [Mrs Bristowe] is alarmingly ill.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [23 April 1829]
letters.summary: CD’s sister Catherine has informed him of the death of WDF’s sister [Mrs Bristowe]. CD sends sympathy to WDF and his parents, and refers to the pure and holy comfort afforded by the Bible.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [18 May 1829]
letters.summary:
Is getting the information WDF wanted about his bills;

adds some news of entomology.

Accepts invitation to visit Osmaston in August. Plans a June trip to Shrewsbury, a three-week trip in Wales with F. W. Hope.

Is doing nothing but riding and entomology.

Thinks WDF wise to defer going into orders.

letters.title: From Francis Knyvett Leighton    [3 June 1829]
letters.summary: Invites CD for the boatrace and the cricket matches, and to see Oxford. Suggests Cambridge will win, but he will bet up to £5 on Oxford at 3 to 1.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    7 June [1829]
letters.summary:
Has shipped a portmanteau and box of WDF’s things. Lists bills paid from funds sent.

"My success has been very splendid in the science" [entomology].

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [3 July 1829]
letters.summary: CD started on an entomology trip through N. Wales with F. W. Hope, but after two days his lips became bad, and he was unwell; had to return home. Took some good insects in the two days, but Hope "did wonders". CD is determined to retrace Hope’s tour before autumn.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [15 July 1829]
letters.summary:
Tells whereabouts of WDF’s remaining Cambridge possessions;

adds he has many insects for him. Can WDF join him for a week in Wales?

CD must read for his "Little Go" as the examination is being made more difficult.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    29 [July 1829]
letters.summary:
Sends stuffed birds;

attempts to arrange a meeting.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    26 [August 1829]
letters.summary: If convenient, CD will visit WDF at Osmaston early in September. Went to Barmouth with his sisters.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    4 September [1829]
letters.summary: Must shorten his visit to Osmaston in order to see Erasmus Darwin, who has just come home.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [22 September 1829]
letters.summary:
Erasmus has changed his plans, intends to give up doctoring for the present, and will live in London.

CD will go to the Birmingham Music Meeting.

He hopes WDF has been finding insects; J. F. Turner has.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox    [15 October 1829]
letters.summary:
The Music Meeting was "glorious"; Malibran outshone all others.

Missed Hope in London.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [3 November 1829]
letters.summary:
CD’s father has been very ill, but is now slowly improving.

Writes of Leonard Jenyns’ cabinet and J. S. Henslow’s parties.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [3 January 1830]
letters.summary:
Spent three weeks in London with Erasmus.

Entomologised with Hope, Stephens, and G. R. Waterhouse.

Cambridge is very quiet, men reading at a wonderful pace. Dined with Sir J. Mackintosh.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [13 January 1830]
letters.summary: Has ordered a cabinet for his insects; hopes WDF will soon come to Cambridge to see his collection. Has exchanged specimens with Leonard Jenyns.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   27 January [1830]
letters.summary: Had an enjoyable week at "Darwin Hotel" during Hunt Week, with two balls, etc., but missed CD.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [25 March 1830]
letters.summary: CD has passed his "Little Go".

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [1 April 1830]
letters.summary:
CD will remain in Cambridge during the whole vacation.

J. F. Stephens has been ill; hence no recent publications.

Has seen a good deal of J. S. Henslow.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [9 May 1830]
letters.summary:
Very sorry WDF was obliged to go to Cheltenham with his parents instead of coming to Cambridge, for the weather is fine, the beetles numerous. Adds news of friends and facts about his collection of insects.

Thinks of reading divinity with Henslow the summer after next.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [31 May 1830]
letters.summary:
Glad WDF will visit him in Shrewsbury.

Hope visited CD; he and T. C. Eyton want CD to join them on an entomological trip to N. Wales; can WDF come?

William Yarrell has discovered a new wild swan in England; CD has had bad specimen of it stuffed for WDF.

Adds brief news of friends.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   25 [August 1830]
letters.summary:
Has been in N. Wales two weeks, having gone with Hope and two Eytons. Not many good insects; disillusioned with Hope, found him egotistical and stupid.

Hopes WDF will stay in Cambridge until after CD arrives.

Some entomological news.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [8 September 1830]
letters.summary:
Very sorry to hear bad news of Mrs Fox.

Shooting not good, but has done some entomology.

Has enjoyed Maer.

Has a horse which he thinks will make a very good hunter.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [8 September 1830]
letters.summary:
Papa has been expecting CD to come and slay some partridges.

Has heard CD has a horse 18½ hands high.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   4 October [1830]
letters.summary: News of family, friends, horses.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [8 October 1830]
letters.summary:
All at Shrewsbury glad to hear good news of Mrs Fox.

CD left Tuesday by coach and two days’ horseback ride to Cambridge. Goes to the Henslows’ that night.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   5 November [1830]
letters.summary:
CD finds the reading involved in "getting up all my subjects" almost "intolerable"; has had no time to write, or send insects, or catch any.

Glad WDF has heard of a curacy where he may "read all the commandments without endangering [his] throat".

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [27? November 1830]
letters.summary:
CD reading very hard for his examination.

Too busy for beetles.

Trusts WDF will be in orders by Christmas.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [23 January 1831]
letters.summary:
Congratulates WDF on passing his examination for the curacy; hopes he will find it comfortable.

CD is pleased at his own good showing.

Asks about WDF’s examination, books, etc.

letters.title: From George Simpson   [26] January [1831]
letters.summary: Congratulates CD on his "very very good degree". Asks about friends; wishes him well.

letters.title: From Henry Matthew   [2 February 1831]
letters.summary: Is in London living in a garret, almost penniless, and has legal and marital difficulties. He hopes to sell some verse.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [9 February 1831]
letters.summary: Will leave Cambridge shortly after division; plans to return for next term. With so many friends, Henslow among the foremost, it will be pleasant.

letters.title: From Henry Matthew   [14 February 1831]
letters.summary: Accepted CD’s "generous remittance" rather than go to jail; has pawned his watch. Will stay one fortnight to see whether he can do anything; if he fails he will go home. If he succeeds he will ask his father to pay his debts and nothing else for a two-year period. Is proud of the attachment CD shows.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [15 February 1831]
letters.summary:
Informs WDF of a shipment of birds ready to be sent by Baker.

Urges WDF to read Herschel’s essay [A preliminary discourse on the study of natural philosophy(1830)] in Lardner’s [Cabinet]Cyclopedia.

letters.title: From Henry Matthew   [March or April 1831]
letters.summary: In London HM was too harassed by his wife to write; has gone home and is much bothered by his father. Looks for a place as a private tutor. Remains CD’s devoted friend.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [7 April 1831]
letters.summary:
CD expects pleasant spring term; will botanise with Henslow.

He is dreaming of going to the Canary Islands for tropical scenery.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [8 April 1831]
letters.summary: Wants CD to come without fail on Monday, and to bring her a small bottle of oil colour, a half-dozen small brushes, and a "juicy" book of some kind.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   [28 April 1831]
letters.summary:
Had a pleasant week in London and is now enjoying Cambridge, where he is busy with work and social engagements.

Writes with great enthusiasm of his prospective trip to "the Tropics" [Canary Islands]. Henslow will cram him in geology. He is working regularly at Spanish.

letters.title: From [J. M. Herbert][early May 1831]
letters.summary:
Asks CD to accept a Coddington microscope, which accompanies his anonymous note.

Compliments CD on talent and sincerity.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [11 May 1831]
letters.summary:
CD’s father has given him £200 to settle his debts.

He is delighted by a magnificent anonymous gift of a microscope.

Sees a good deal of the Henslows who are expecting a child soon.

CD still talks of the "Canary scheme"; he is learning Spanish.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [9 July 1831]
letters.summary:
Poverty keeps him at Shrewsbury.

The Canary scheme still goes, CD is studying Spanish and geology.

Jenyns has started CD on Diptera.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [11 July 1831]
letters.summary:
Has been learning to use a clinometer.

Has investigated passage and fares for Canaries trip.

Rereading Humboldt.

Asks JSH to thank Jenyns for present of Diptera.

letters.title: To C. T. Whitley    [19 July 1831]
letters.summary:
He is "mad about Geology" and plans to ride through Wales in August with a few days at Barmouth.

Some humorous gossip.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   1 August [1831]
letters.summary:
Will send his insects and two or three from Henslow.

The Canary scheme takes place next June.

Is grieved WDF thinks him capable of telling falsehoods.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   24 August 1831
letters.summary: JSH has been asked by Peacock to recommend a naturalist as companion to Capt. FitzRoy onBeaglevoyage. CD the best qualified person; not a finished naturalist but amply qualified for collecting, observing, and noting.

letters.title: From George Peacock   [c.26 August 1831]
letters.summary: Details about FitzRoy and proposed voyage ofBeagle. CD invited to go on the voyage as naturalist.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   30 [August 1831]
letters.summary:
Feels he should declineBeaglevoyage offer because of his father’s objections, which he lists. Would otherwise have taken all risks.

[Geological] trip with Adam Sedgwick a success.

Grieved at Marmaduke Ramsay’s death.

letters.title: To R. W. Darwin   31 August [1831]
letters.summary: CD asks his father to consider the offer of theBeaglevoyage once more. He encloses his list of RWD’s objections and Josiah Wedgwood’s responses [see109]. Asks his father to give him a decided answer: if "no" he will never again mention the subject.

letters.title: To Francis Beaufort   1 September [1831]
letters.summary: CD accepts going with Capt. FitzRoy. Explains earlier refusal as owing to his father’s disapproval.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [2 September 1831]
letters.summary: Has just arrived in Cambridge; his father has changed his mind. Asks to see JSH.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   [4 September 1831]
letters.summary: Spent preceding day with Henslow; much to be done. A friend, Alexander Charles Wood, has written to Capt. FitzRoy about CD. Peacock offered appointment asBeaglenaturalist first to Leonard Jenyns, who almost accepted, as did Henslow himself. CD will talk to Capt. Francis Beaufort [Hydrographer] and FitzRoy. Thanks all his family.

letters.title: From Adam Sedgwick   4 September 1831
letters.summary: Reports on his geological work in N. Wales since he and CD parted. Answers CD’s queries.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   [5 September 1831]
letters.summary: Wood has heard from FitzRoy, who seemed so much against CD’s going that CD and Henslow gave up. CD is in London; has seen FitzRoy, who is now ready to invite him. CD remains undecided. He likes FitzRoy. Gives details of prospective arrangements. They probably will be gone three years; "round the world" is not certain. Want of room is a serious objection.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [5 September 1831]
letters.summary: Has met FitzRoy, who has now offered him the post of naturalist on board theBeagle. Other details about the voyage arrangements – mess, CD’s status, route, books.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   [6 September 1831]
letters.summary: Orders clothing, books, and other supplies for the voyage, to be sent to him in London.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   6 [September 1831]
letters.summary:
Received offer of post as naturalist in theBeaglein the same mail as WDF’s last letter. Outlines details of prospective voyage. Not certain, but thinks he probably will go.

Expresses pleasure that all is well with their friendship, which he prizes.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   [9 September 1831]
letters.summary:
Discusses help he is receiving in his preparations for the voyage from William Yarrell and others. He has ordered a case of pistols, a rifle, and a good telescope with compass. It is settled that he will go.

Describes the coronation of William IV.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   9 [September 1831]
letters.summary: All is settled – nothing can now alter CD’s determination. Details of plan and arrangements. Beaufort believes CD’s collections should be presented to some public body. CD thinks a large central collection best for natural history. Is busy getting advice and information from Yarrell and Capt. P. P. King for the voyage.

letters.title: To Charles Whitley   [9 September 1831]
letters.summary: Mentions letters from Peacock and Henslow; tells of offer of a position on surveying voyage, his initial refusal, and eventual acceptance. Describes FitzRoy and course of voyage.

letters.title: From John Coldstream   13 September 1831
letters.summary: Suggestions and information helpful to CD in preparation forBeaglevoyage. David Brewster’s meteorological papers. Suggests an oyster-trawl for collecting marine animals. Recommends CD see R. E. Grant. For meteorological observations suggests F. W. Beechey’sVoyage to the Pacific[1831] and an interview with J. F. Daniell of King’s College.

letters.title: From Charles Whitley   13 September 1831
letters.summary: Congratulates CD onBeagleappointment as an "opportunity … of studying all the natural sciences at once, after your own taste".

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   [14 September 1831]
letters.summary: Pleasant three-day voyage to Plymouth has increased CD’s admiration for FitzRoy. Describes theBeagleas an excellent vessel, but the want of room is very bad. He likes the officers.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   17 [September 1831]
letters.summary:
Plans to come to Shrewsbury.

Is pleased with cabin assignment onBeagle.Beaglewill map the east side of Tierra del Fuego and Patagonia and set longitude of many places.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   17 [September 1831]
letters.summary: Plans to come to Cambridge to discussBeaglevoyage. Only difficulty is disposal of his collections. South Sea Islands now more probable.

letters.title: From Adam Sedgwick   18 September 1831
letters.summary:
Is glad of CD’s appointment and hopes it will be a source of happiness and honour.

Answers a query about books.

Suggests CD go to Geological Society, present himself, as AS’s friend, to William Lonsdale and study the Society’s collection.

Tells CD of his work in Wales; includes a diagram and explanations.

Ramsay’s death a grievous loss.

letters.title: From Frederick Watkins   [18 September 1831]
letters.summary:
Rejoices in CD’s appointment and predicts he will rank with Candolle, Henslow, and Linnaeus.

Recounts their past pleasures and gives news of friends, who are scattering fast.

letters.title: To Robert FitzRoy   [19 September 1831]
letters.summary: Reports on errands he has done for RF. Has discussed with Beaufort the question of his having right to dispose of his collection.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   19 [September 1831]
letters.summary: Describes his appointment, theBeagle, his companions, and the objectives of the voyage. Gives his schedule before departure.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [22 September – 2 October 1831]
letters.summary: Sends him a purse, which she asks him to use in remembrance of her.

letters.title: From Charlotte Wedgwood   22 September [1831]
letters.summary: Sends congratulations and good wishes; feels the Wedgwoods bear much responsibility, since he would not have accepted theBeagleappointment had he not been at Maer "that 1st. of September".

letters.title: From Robert FitzRoy   23 September 1831
letters.summary: Regrets he cannot take Francis Owen onBeagleas midshipman. RF thinks CD had better be on the books [for victuals], but CD should do as he likes. Refitting progress is slow.

letters.title: To Charles Whitley   23 [September 1831]
letters.summary:
Thanks CTW for his letter [125]. "I do not think I ever received a more kind letter than yours or one that gave me so much pleasure.— You ought to have in your mind, the prospect of leaving England for 3 or 4 years before you can understand how to enjoy such a letter from such a person as yourself—". Regarding the voyage, "all is finally settled, & I have sealed away about half a chance of life.— If one lived merely to see how long one could spin out life,—I should repent my choice.— As it is I do not.—"

Thanks CTW for four fungi which have arrived.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [26 September 1831]
letters.summary: Much disappointed that CD will leave home before she returns.

letters.title: From Sarah Owen   [27–30 September 1831]
letters.deprecated: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.sender: Sarah Harriet (Sarah Harriet Williams) (Sarah Harriet Mostyn Owen) Haliburton
letters.summary: She encloses a pin with "genuine hair" and is flattered that it will go around the world with CD.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   28 [September 1831]
letters.summary:
Has collected [Phalli] in Shropshire and compared them with Barmouth species. Is convinced they are different.

Asks JSH for introductions to R. T. Lowe and Andrew Smith.

Has been given another week’s respite by FitzRoy.

letters.title: To Robert FitzRoy   [4 or 11 October 1831]
letters.summary:
CD’s luggage is frightfully bulky, though he has been as economical as possible. Has made financial arrangements for his expenses.

Plans to study mathematics during voyage.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [4 or 11 October 1831]
letters.summary: Asks JSH to take charge of his consignments of specimens from the voyage.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen   [6 October 1831]
letters.summary: Their letters crossed; she now knows he will be gone for three years, not two; does not know what they will do without him at the Forest, but wishes him well.

letters.title: To Robert FitzRoy [10 October 1831]
letters.summary: Has just heardBeaglesailing is delayed so he will remain another week in London. Asks whether RF has a good set of mountain barometers, which geologists tell him are important.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   25 October 1831
letters.summary:
Gives CD directions for sending him specimens fromBeagle.

Writes of Cambridge politics.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   30 [October 1831]
letters.summary:
Hopes to be able to help Cambridge Philosophical Society with his collections, but thinks most will have to go to British Museum.

DescribesBeaglequarters, the surgeon [Robert McCormick, M.D.], and officers.

Asks JSH’s advice on studying mathematics.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   [31?] October [1831]
letters.summary:
Questions about his college bills.

Describes the living conditions he will have on theBeagle.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   12 November [1831]
letters.summary:
The outfitting of theBeagleprogresses.

CD has been dining out more than he wishes. He has met W. S. Harris of "Electricity" fame.

His fears and hopes about seasickness.

A new continent has been discovered "somewhere far South". "Perhaps we may be sent in search."

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow    15 [November 1831]
letters.summary: Sailing date fixed for end of month.Beagleis beautiful. Details of instructions and route. Hopes voyage will not exceed four years. Quarters very confined. Considers Jenyns did wisely in not coming. If CD were longer out of college and some years older he never could have endured it.

letters.title: To Charles Whitley    15 November [1831]
letters.summary:
Regrets that it will be impossible to visit Cambridge for some years. Reminisces about CW’s "classical Sunday evenings", the Glutton Club, and his friends.

"We spend about 2 years in S. America, the rest of time larking round the world."

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   17 [November 1831]
letters.summary: Still delayed; will not sail until 5 December. Instructions have come, with proposed itinerary.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   20 November 1831
letters.summary:
Is sending plates for R. T. Lowe’s paper [Trans. Cambridge Philos. Soc.4 (1833): 1–70].

Adds advice on working the surd.

Agrees with CD thatBeaglevoyage would have been wrong for Jenyns, but assures him he (CD) is the right man. Warns CD against his "foible" of taking offence at rudeness or ungentlemanlike behaviour.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen    2 [December 1831]
letters.summary: Describes the wedding of her sister Sarah and related festivities. She misses CD very much.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow    3 December [1831]
letters.summary: Confusion on board theBeagleat definite prospect of sailing. Gives directions for sending mail to Montevideo.

letters.title: From Caroline, Catherine, and Susan Darwin 20–31 December [1831]
letters.deprecated: Caroline Sarah DarwinEmily Catherine (Catherine) LangtonSusan Elizabeth Darwin
letters.sender: Caroline Sarah DarwinEmily Catherine (Catherine) LangtonSusan Elizabeth Darwin
letters.summary: Family and Shropshire news.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   8 January – 4 February 1832
letters.summary: News of family and friends, much of it about forthcoming marriages: Fanny Owen and R. M. Biddulph, Fanny Mackintosh and Hensleigh Wedgwood. Charlotte Wedgwood will write to him of her own engagement to Charles Langton.

letters.title: From Charlotte Wedgwood   12 January – 1 February 1832
letters.summary: Writes about Hensleigh Wedgwood’s marriage to Frances Mackintosh and her own engagement to Charles Langton. Also gives news of other relatives and friends.

letters.title: From Bartholomew James Sulivan  E [17 January – 7 February 1832]
letters.summary: Heights of various points on Quail Island [Cape Verde Is.].

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow    6 February 1832
letters.summary: News of Cambridge: the recent examinations; memorial tablet for Marmaduke Ramsay.

letters.title: To R. W. Darwin   10 February 1832
letters.summary:
Sends a short résumé of his trip on the chance that it will arrive in England earlier than longer letter [158] which he hopes to send by surer means.

He is "incessantly occupied by new and most interesting animals" and thinks he will be able to do some original work in natural history.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   12 February [– 3 March] 1832
letters.summary: Chronicles the events of February, principally of the family and of a few friends: engagements, marriages, deaths, some visits.

letters.title: To R. W. Darwin 8 February – 1 March 1832
letters.summary: Writes with great happiness about the first part of the voyage, after his misery from seasickness passed. He finds himself well prepared, the ship quiet, comfortable, and compact; he has already a "rich harvest" and finds the natural history (especially geology) exceedingly interesting. The tropics are full of great beauty.

letters.title: From Fanny Owen    1 March 1832
letters.summary: Writes affectionately of the good times they have had and of her friendship for CD. Tells him of her forthcoming marriage to R. M. Biddulph.

letters.title: From William Mostyn Owen Sr    1 March 1832
letters.summary: Writes of his family and Shropshire events. Comments on the slow progress of the Reform Bill.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   (with postscript by Marianne Parker) 12[–29] March [1832]
letters.summary: Describes the gathering at Maer and the events culminating in Charlotte Wedgwood’s marriage to Charles Langton.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin    2–6 April 1832
letters.summary: CD’s enjoyment of the beauty of the tropics is worth all the misery of seasickness. His mail gave him great pleasure. For two weeks he will visit a large estate in the country, and on return live at Botofogo for some weeks, collecting and learning to know the tropics.

letters.title: From J. M. Herbert 15–17 April 1832
letters.summary: Writes news of Cambridge friends, professors, music, the Reform Bill, and cholera. Expresses belief that CD will take his place with Cuvier and Humboldt.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin    25–6 April [1832]
letters.summary: His trip to the interior was full of interest, but exhausting physically. Expects to stay at least a fortnight at Botofogo, because theBeaglereturns to Bahia to correct a difference in the longitude measurements. Writes of his companions, of FitzRoy, and of his journal – which he has sent home.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   26–7 April [1832]
letters.summary: Writes chiefly of family affairs: Erasmus’ visit, further delay in Fanny Owen’s marriage, Sarah [Owen] Williams’ illness, Arthur Owen’s sad departure for India; cholera.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   May 1832
letters.summary: Writes of voyage and his work in natural history: geology, collecting insects (freshwater beetles and spiders at Botofogo Bay); life at sea, sublime views ashore.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin May–June [1832]
letters.summary:
Lists letters received and those sent; comments on family happenings.

TheBeagleis back [from Bahia]; two sailors and "little [Charles] Musters" died of fever. In 14 days they sail for Montevideo, then to Rio Negro, then on to where no man is known to have been before.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   12 May [– 2 June] 1832
letters.summary:
News from Maer and Shrewsbury of family, friends, and reports of reactions to CD’s first letters.

Sedgwick suggests he look for fossils in gravel banks of rivers.

Fanny Owen is married to R. M. Biddulph. Reform Bill prospects.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   18 May – 16 June 1832
letters.summary: His first letter to JSH since December. Recounts his seasickness, geologising and marine collecting at St Jago [Santiago, Cape Verde Is.]; his first tropical forest. Collecting small insects from the tropics. His Welsh trip with Sedgwick has been extremely valuable.

letters.title: To J. M. Herbert   [1–6] June 1832
letters.summary: Summarises experiences since leaving England. "How intimately what may be called the ""moral part"" is connected with the enjoyment of scenery." The loneliness of the voyage.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   12–28 June [1832]
letters.summary: Brings CD up to date on family and many friends. Describes the wedding of Fanny Owen and R. M. Biddulph. Sedgwick called on return from Wales. W. D. Fox has been very ill.

letters.title: From W. D. Fox 30 June 1832
letters.summary: Has been away from parish because of a three-month illness. Refers briefly to events in England since theBeaglesailed.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   5 July [1832]
letters.summary:
Sailing next day to Montevideo. He has taken many hitherto undescribed animals. Describes the glories of the Brazilian forest.

Mentions his concern over the Reform Bill.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   14 July – 7 August [1832]
letters.summary: Regrets leaving the tropics, despite interest in a land where Europeans have never been. They have experienced political turmoil at Montevideo. Natural history going well.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [23 July –] 15 August [1832]
letters.summary: Specimens being sent off. Describes his collection of rocks, plants, and insects. Some particularly interesting specimens.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   25 July [– 3 August] 1832
letters.summary:
Tells of the family’s pleasure in reading CD’s first two letters and his journal.

Comments on Shrewsbury politics, the cholera, and the family. Sedgwick calls often; Catherine thinks he is interested in Susan.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   15[–18] August 1832
letters.summary: News of family and friends.

letters.title: From E. A. Darwin 18 August [1832]
letters.summary: Reports on the commissions CD requested of him [in a missing letter]; comments on English political issues.

letters.title: To Frederick Watkins   18 August 1832
letters.summary: Brief summary of the voyage so far. His delight in the Brazilian forest; his trip into the interior; the turbulence at Rio; has grown a beard.

letters.title: From Sarah Williams    26[–31] August 1832
letters.summary: Gives CD an "account of my life and adventures since we parted" and news of her family.

letters.title: From W. D. Fox   29 August – 28 September 1832
letters.summary:
He is staying on the Isle of Wight because he has been unwell. He is thought to be in danger of contracting consumption, and the climate is beneficial. He is convalescent now, but will spend the winter there.

Offers to forward any natural history stores CD may want.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   12[–18] September 1832
letters.summary: News of the Darwin, Wedgwood, and Owen families, including a report on Frances Wedgwood’s death.

letters.title: From Charlotte Langton   27 [September] 1832
letters.summary:
Rejoices in what she hears of his voyage and his pleasures in it.

Writes of her new life, and of their relatives and friends.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   14 October [1832]
letters.summary:
Writes news of family, Maer, and Woodhouse. His father has sent for a banana tree

and plans to buy J. J. Audubon’s book [Birds of America(1827)].

Charles Langton has been given a living near Ludlow.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   24 October – 24 November [1832]
letters.summary:
During the past two months CD has been lucky with fossil bones, and he is also finding new specimens of living animals.

He describes an ostrich hunt.

Has received several letters from home.

He enjoys Buenos Aires and admires the señoritas. Tierra del Fuego is next.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [c.26 October –] 24 November [1832]
letters.summary: A French collector [Alcide d’Orbigny] has been at the Rio Negro and will probably have "taken the cream". CD’s luck with fossil bones, among them a large extinct armadillo-like animal. Describes some birds, toads, Crustacea, and other marine specimens. Nearly all plants flowering at Bahia Blanca were collected. Is sending two large casks of fossil bones by packet.

letters.title: From Charles Hughes   2 November [1832]
letters.summary: Notes for CD on a river trip to Mercedes on the Rio Negro [Uruguay].

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [12–13] November 1832
letters.summary:
Sketches theBeagle’s travels – Rio de Janeiro, Montevideo, cruise to the south and return – and what the future holds. Writes with nostalgia of England and says he sees no end to the voyage.

He enjoys and has been lucky principally in geology and among pelagic animals; has found remains of large extinct animals.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   12–18 November 1832
letters.summary: Family news.

letters.title: From J. M. Herbert   1[–4] December 1832
letters.summary: Sends news of himself and CD’s friends. Discusses changes in England, the coming elections, Cambridge politics.

letters.title: From Robert FitzRoy   [1833?]
letters.summary: List of mountains with their heights.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   13 January 1833
letters.summary: Family news. Uncle Jos [Josiah Wedgwood II] has been returned to Parliament with a fine majority.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   15–21 January 1833
letters.summary:
Acknowledges receipt of two letters from CD and a box of specimens.

Mentions attendance at BAAS meeting and a gift to him of a small living near Oxford. Some political news.

Congratulates CD on the work he has done – the specimens are of great interest. Gives advice on packing, labelling, and future collecting and suggests that – as a precaution – CD send home a copy of his notes on the specimens.

letters.title: From W. D. Fox   23 January 1833
letters.summary:
His health has improved but he continues "a good deal of an invalid" and is uncertain what the future holds for him.

His interest in entomology and ornithology continues; he has been studying the gulls on the Isle of Wight.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   3–6 March 1833
letters.summary:
Captain Beaufort has offered to get one more letter to CD before the long voyage around the Horn;

SD brings family news up to date.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   7 March [1833]
letters.summary: Sends her love and family news.

letters.title: From R. W. Darwin   7 March 1833
letters.summary:
Writes of the pleasure all feel in CD’s continued good health and joy in his voyage.

Tells of the banana tree he bought, which he sits under and thinks of CD "in similar shade".

CD’s financial accounts are correct.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   30 March – 12 April 1833
letters.summary: Account of the four-month voyage to Tierra del Fuego, Cape Horn, and return. The Fuegians are landed with Richard Matthews [the missionary in charge of them]. Storms, seasickness, hostile savages, and scenery are described. His increasing interest in all branches of natural history makes the hardships worth while. FitzRoy buys a schooner. CD will stay at Rio Negro while it is fitted.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   11 April 1833
letters.summary:
Description of the months at Tierra del Fuego. His first sight of the primitive Fuegians. Geological and zoological observations and specimens.

The Falklands: geological and zoological observations.

Convinced the [Megatherium] sent to Royal College of Physicians [by Woodbine Parish] belongs to same formation as bones he sent home.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   1–4 May 1833
letters.summary: News of family and friends.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   22 May – 14 July 1833
letters.summary:
Longs to be on the other side of the Horn; tired of these countries. Natural history makes him continue. He now knows it will remain his favourite pursuit for the rest of his life.

Comments on slavery.

Will have additional space on board and a servant [Syms Covington] who will help him with the collection of birds and quadrupeds.

Asks for books, a lens, and four pairs of shoes.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   23 May 1833
letters.summary:
He misses society. "I often conjecture what will become of me; my wishes certainly would make me a country clergyman. – You expect sadly more than I shall ever do in Nat. Hist: I am only a sort of Jackall, a lions provider; but I wish I was sure there were lions enough."

Has collected a host of minute beetles, some reptiles, small quadrupeds, and fishes. Invertebrate marine animals are his delight. The pleasure of working with microscope ranks second only to geology.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   29 May 1833
letters.summary: She and Susan are in London, and she writes of people they have seen or had news of: Captain Harding, E. A. Darwin, Fanny [Mrs Hensleigh] Wedgwood, Emma Wedgwood, the Langtons, Josiah Wedgwood and Aunt Bessie, Fanny Biddulph and child, and the Evanses of Portrane.

letters.title: J. M. Herbert   2 June 1833
letters.summary:
Describes Tierra del Fuego and Cape Horn; was reminded of hours at Barmouth; chafes at the length of the trip.

Hopes the Whigs will do away with slavery – has seen enough of it and Negroes to be disgusted with the lies heard in England.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   18 July 1833
letters.summary:
Fears JSH will think his collections scanty. Makes it a constant rule to prefer obscure and diminutive tribes of animals.

Now has a servant whom he has taught to skin birds, etc.

Lists four barrels of specimens he is sending.

Gives future route. He looks forward to the western coast of South America.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   22–31 July 1833
letters.summary: News of family and friends after skipping June letter: Osmaston and the Foxes, five weeks in London, the Langtons in Shropshire, Fanny Biddulph and daughter, R. W. Darwin, and Charles Hughes.

letters.title: From Robert FitzRoy   24 [August 1833]
letters.summary: Wishes CD well on his trip to General Juan Manuel Rosas. CD is to send word when he wants a boat; there is no hurry, for there is plenty of work for the sounders. He envies CD’s travels.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   31 August 1833
letters.summary:
The [Megatherium] fossils were extremely interesting and were shown at the Geological Section of the BAAS meeting at Cambridge [1833].

The plants delight him; will work them out with W. J. Hooker.

CD should send every fossil he can find; minute insects will be nearly all new. Delighted with descriptions of the few animals alluded to.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   1 September 1833
letters.summary: News of family and friends. "I tell you all the gossip I can that you may know how the Shropshire world is going on."

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [20–7] September 1833
letters.summary: Informs JSH that a Spanish friend has offered him a cargo of bones. If they arrive, he has arranged with Edward Lumb to forward them to JSH. [Forwarded to JSH with244.]

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   20 September [1833]
letters.summary: With the help of General Rosas, CD has just finished an overland journey from Patagones to Buenos Aires; he tells of fossil finds at Bahia Blanca and Guardia del Monte. Spring reminds him of home.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   27 September 1833
letters.summary: Mainly Shropshire news of family and friends.

letters.title: From Robert FitzRoy   4 October 1833
letters.summary: Urges CD to return to theBeagleearly in November. Conrad Martens arrives to succeed Augustus Earle as artist for the expedition.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   15 October 1833
letters.summary: Mainly news of the family and friends. Their joy at the abolition of slavery.

letters.title: From Fanny Myddelton Biddulph   [c. 21 October 1833]
letters.summary: Shropshire news of relatives and friends.

letters.title: From Sarah Williams   21 October 1833
letters.summary: News of Fanny Biddulph and other Owens; Susan Darwin has declined a marriage offer. Other gossip about Shrewsbury acquaintances.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   23 [October 1833]
letters.summary: Describes his trip to north of Santa Fé, his illness, and return by boat to Buenos Aires – which he found in the throes of a revolution. Covington is cut off from the town, which some expect to be plundered.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   25 October 1833
letters.summary: Writes of his ride from Rio Negro to Bahia Blanca and Buenos Aires, which he undertook in order to learn the geology of the land, so full of bones of large extinct quadrupeds.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   28 October [1833]
letters.summary:
Finds CD’s journal very entertaining and interesting, but thinks his style in first part too much influenced by Humboldt.

Sends some books by Harriet Martineau and Archbishop Whately.

Rejoices that the more he sees of Negroes, the better he thinks of them.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   29 October 1833
letters.summary: Finds his journal interesting; they will read it aloud to Papa on winter evenings. They all regret the long time the journey is taking.

letters.title: From Henry Stephen Fox   31 October 1833
letters.summary:
Urges CD to visit Flores Island near Montevideo if he has not already done so. Describes formation of greenstone and the granite formations on small islands in the Uruguay channel.

Sends specimens from Pôrto Alegre [Brazil] for identification by CD.

letters.title: To Frederick William Hope   1 November 1833
letters.summary: Tierra del Fuego and the barren coasts of Patagonia are "singularly unfavourable to the insect world". In the tropics, however, CD captured minute Coleoptera by the hundreds – which should result in his bringing home many undescribed species.

letters.title: From Thomas Campbell Eyton   12 November 1833
letters.summary:
Has been working hard on collecting English and foreign birds. Yarrell has written of new birds discovered in England.

News of work in progress by Leonard Jenyns, P. J. Selby, and John Gould.

Cautions CD to beware of insects when he sends any birds’ skins – otherwise there will be only feathers, beaks, and legs remaining when he returns.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   12 November 1833
letters.summary:
Is sending a cargo of specimens – birds’ skins, small quadrupeds, and fossil bones.

Describes his overland trip from Rio Negro to Buenos Aires and his expedition to Santa Fé.

Asks for mineralogical works to help him with the volcanic rocks of the west coast.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   13 November 1833
letters.summary:
His troubles during the revolution have ended well.

Now plans to investigate geological formations at Rio Negro. Is concerned about the expense but cannot bear to miss seeing "one of the most curious pieces of Geology".

letters.title: From Edward Lumb   13 November 1833
letters.summary: Sending shot or powder is illegal, but all CD’s goods and chattels have been sent. EL’s services to CD are what any Englishman should do for his country.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   27 November 1833
letters.summary:
Mentions letters sent in parcel and those from CD received by Fox and Henslow. Adds news of family and friends.

Appreciation of his journal. She hears that CD’s "theory of the Earth" is the same as Lyell’s in 3d volume [ofPrinciples of geology(1833)].

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   3 December [1833]
letters.summary:
Has had to draw bills totalling £217 in seven months.

Is glad the Captain has decided to winter in Tierra del Fuego, because this will facilitate "glorious excursions" into the Andes.

Has obtained fragments of fossil bones and part of aMegatheriumhead.

Their long delay occurred because the charts were not complete for sending home.

CD is now on shore because of seasickness.

The family may not hear from him for a year.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   30 December [1833] – 3 January 1834
letters.summary: News of family and friends. Hensleigh Wedgwood’s scruples about swearing oaths.

letters.title: From F. W. Hope   15 January 1834
letters.summary:
Acknowledges CD’s letter about alpine entomology of Tierra del Fuego; discusses geographical distribution; urges CD to make a chart of vegetable and geological distribution of insects. Advises him on species to collect and assures him of all assistance in describing his captures on his return.

Tells of founding of Entomological Society, and enrolls CD.

News of J. F. Stephens’ lawsuit and continuation of hisIllustrations of British entomology[1827–46]. Praises general state of zoological science in England.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   27–30 January 1834
letters.summary: News of family and friends: W. D. Fox will marry in the spring; private theatricals at Eaton house-party.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   12[–28] February 1834
letters.summary:
Writes on CD’s 25th birthday.

Points out "errors in orthography" in his journal.

News of family and friends, visits, and other social events.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   March 1834
letters.summary:
On fossils ([Megatherium], etc.), plants, shells sent and new ones found; geological observations. Asks for help in understanding cleavage and planes of deposition.

A new species of ostrich. Cites differences in size, colour, nidification, and geographical distribution.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   9–28 March [1834]
letters.summary:
They learn from a garbled report in theTimesthat CD’s specimens have arrived in Cambridge.

William Clift, at Royal College of Surgeons, delighted by CD’s letter about the bones that were sent to Plymouth.

Strange coincidence that Royal College of Surgeons has the front portion and CD has sent home the remainder of a skull, of which a drawing can now be completed.

Other news of family and friends.

letters.title: From J. M. Herbert   [28 March] 1834
letters.summary: A letter full of news of Cambridge and friends: the BAAS meeting at Cambridge; charges of corruption in the University; the Cambridge petition on behalf of Dissenters.

letters.title: To Edward Lumb   30 March 1834
letters.summary:
CD asks the time of shipment and vessel in which the [Megatherium] bones were conveyed.

Patagonia swarms with guanaco, but few other creatures.

Hopes to be able to draw up a tolerable sketch of the geology of the east side of S. America.

Saw Jemmy Button, who is married and will stay in Tierra del Fuego. Mentions Falkland uprising.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   6 April 1834
letters.summary:
Describes Patagonia and its inhabitants.

Writes of his pleasure in geology.

Predicts that Falklands will become an "important halting place". OutlinesBeagle’s future itinerary.

letters.title: From William Owen Sr   10 April – 1 May 1834
letters.summary:
Writes a cordial letter with family and local news. Hopes CD will see his two sons in India.

P.S. by Catherine Darwin says no letter was written this month as all is well at home.

letters.title: From Edward Lumb   8 May 1834
letters.summary:
Responds to CD’s queries: the bones were received from Mr Keen and shipped to Henslow; expects another collection which he will forward.

Adds news that has arrived at Buenos Aires since CD left.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   [23] May 1834
letters.summary: News of family and friends.

letters.title: From Robert Edward Alison   [June? 1834]
letters.summary: Sends some historical data to illustrate the elevation of the coast at Valparaiso in recent times.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   20–9 July 1834
letters.summary:
In the past six months he has done much geology and natural history. His geological pursuits are a source of high pleasure. Has lately determined to work chiefly on corals.

Spent three weeks going up the Santa Cruz with a party; they ran out of provisions 20 miles from the Cordilleras. Winter at present prevents his doing much natural history.

letters.title: From J. S. Henslow   22 July 1834
letters.summary:
CD’s cargo is safe; the fossils have been sent to William Clift.

JSH asks for dried plants (those sent were all of greatest interest).

Sends news of Cambridge and mutual friends.

letters.title: To Charles Whitley   23 July 1834
letters.summary:
Would welcome hearing Cambridge news. Impossible not to regret friends and pleasures in England, but

has much solid enjoyment and never-failing interest in geology. Tells of his first sight of a savage.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   24 July – 7 November 1834
letters.summary:
CD is excited by JSH’s high opinion of his collections.

Discusses his notes and some new discoveries. Summary of events since leaving Falklands.

Geology of Patagonia.

Corallines at Tierra del Fuego convince him of artificiality of arrangement of their families by Lamarck and Cuvier.

Geological expedition in Andes, ending with serious illness. Specimens being sent.

letters.title: From H. S. Fox   25 July 1834
letters.summary:
Thanks CD for letter of 5 April and specimens; did not know the Falklands and Patagonia were so interesting geologically.

Will answer CD’s queries about S. Brazil in another letter. Names Friedrich Sellow, A. Saint-Hilaire, and Andrew Mathews as naturalists who travelled there. Directs CD to Alexander Caldcleugh in Santiago.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   9–12 August 1834
letters.summary:
Thanks for her letter of March, which gave him his first explanation of the interest in the [Megatherium] head he had sent.

Wants E. A. Darwin to tell William Clift not to remove numbers or markers on any specimens. The British Museum has first claim on any of his specimens; CD cannot at present say where any should go.

letters.title: From [Alexander Caldcleugh?]   [28 August – 5 September 1834]
letters.summary: Gives a map of part of Chile between Santiago and San Fernando. Suggests places and people that CD might profitably visit [en route].

letters.title: To Robert FitzRoy   [28 August 1834]
letters.summary: Recounts his trip [from Valparaiso] to Santiago. His meeting with Claude Gay, Thomas Sutcliffe, and others. Geology of tour uninteresting.

letters.title: From Frederick W. Eck   [September 1834]
letters.summary: Heights of various places in Chile.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   30 September 1834
letters.summary:
News of family and friends.

Word that William Clift thinks CD’s latest fossils are of much value.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   4 October 1834
letters.summary:
CD is unwell.

FitzRoy has dispatched two casks of bones and stones, a box with "very valuable specimens", and a large jar.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   13 October 1834
letters.summary: Became ill two weeks before on his return from Santiago after an interesting trip and some geology – though snow kept him out of the Andes. FitzRoy has had to sell the schooner; he was discouraged by the Admiralty, and the expense was too much for him to bear personally.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   29 October 1834
letters.summary: Family and local news. Tom Eyton will marry. Tells of the great fire of the Houses of Parliament.

letters.title: From W. D. Fox   1 November 1834
letters.summary: WDF sends news of his activities and of his family.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   8 November 1834
letters.summary: Sends two boxes of specimens and part of his "hum-drum letter-like" journal.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   8 November 1834
letters.summary:
CD has recovered from his illness.

Fatigue and depression had almost decided Captain FitzRoy to turn over his command, but he was dissuaded.

Beaglewill now go no further south than Cape Tres Montes and will finish survey in five months.

CD experiences his first earthquake.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   [24] November 1834
letters.summary: The Langtons will go to Madeira for the winter. E. A. Darwin and the Hensleigh Wedgwoods enjoyed a stay in Cambridge, where they saw Professors Whewell and Sedgwick. Colonel Leighton has died. The King has dismissed the Whig Ministry; Wellington is Premier, and the country is in a strange state.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   29 December [1834]
letters.summary:
Has sent all of CD’s directions to William Clift.

Erasmus has been very ill, but is now quite safe and well again. Caroline and Susan are with him.

They have heard FitzRoy is promoted and theBeagleis coming home.

letters.title: From Caroline and Catherine Darwin   28 January [1835]
letters.summary:
Concerned over CD’s illness. His father strongly urges him to come home lest his health be ruined.

News of family and friends.

Twelve Tories elected in Shropshire.

letters.title: From Charles Whitley   5 February 1835
letters.summary: Replies to CD’s letter [250], giving news of himself and mutual friends.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   16 February 1835
letters.summary:
Met Capt. Harding who said FitzRoy was promoted to Post-Captain.

News of family and friends. Forthcoming marriages of Robert Wedgwood and Tom Eyton.

letters.title: From Charles D. Douglas   24 February 1835
letters.summary:
Sends CD large beetles from Chiloé.

Describes an earthquake at Caucague.

Gives exact location and measurements of two blocks of granite; has seen and heard of others; will report if he surveys the Potrero on Chiloé.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [7–11] March 1835
letters.summary:
Congratulates WDF on his marriage,

reminisces about Cambridge and early entomology. Now neglects entomology for geology.

Describes Concepción after earthquake.

Hopes to cross Cordilleras before they leave South America in September.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   10–13 March 1835
letters.summary:
Definite plans now to leave Valparaiso 1 June and to arrive in Sydney in January; then Cape of Good Hope and home in September 1836.

Describes Concepción after earthquake.

Will cross the Cordilleras. Hopes snow will hold off.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow[10] – 13 March 1835
letters.summary:
The termination of the voyage has been decided – September 1836.

The earthquake of Concepción.

His geological observations (since November). Can now prove both sides of the Andes have recently risen to considerable heights.

Zoological collection.

Plans to cross the Cordilleras.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   30 March 1835
letters.summary: Urges him to return home. News of family and friends; the Langtons will go to Rio in April and then winter in the West Indies. Henslow has a son.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   18 April 1835
letters.summary: Has just returned from crossing the Cordilleras. Geological observations of formations representing great epochs of violence which broke up the earth’s crust. Shells at over 12000 feet. Silicified trees in sandstone formations at great heights. Red snow and viviparous lizards. Botanical specimens.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   23 April 1835
letters.summary: His trip across the Andes and back was his most successful excursion: can clearly demonstate that the western part of the double line of mountains is much older, with fossil shells at 12000ft; the eastern line may be as modern as the Patagonian plains. If proved, this is an important fact in the theory of the formation of the world. Has found petrified trees.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   31 May [1835]
letters.summary: Slow and tedious trip through miserable country, but geology prospers, and CD will have a good general idea of the structure of Chile by the time he leaves the country. Will send a last large cargo of specimens to Henslow.

letters.title: From R. E. Alison   25 June 1835
letters.summary: Gives details of his observations which lend support to the view that Chile is rising with respect to the sea. Reports some observations and opinions with regard to earthquakes and volcanic action in the area.

letters.title: From R. H. Corfield   26–7 June 1835
letters.summary: Greatly enjoyed CD’s company; has worried about his health. Adds some European and English news.

letters.title: From Charles San Lambert   [c.July 1835]
letters.summary: Describes volcanic formations capping granite hills from Copiapò to Atacama [Chile]. [SeeSouth America, pp. 230–1.]

letters.title: From R. H. Corfield 14 — 18 July 1835
letters.summary: Passes on news from England and some Shrewsbury papers.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   [19] July – [12 August] 1835
letters.summary:
Describes his trip from Coquimbo to Copiapò, where he rejoined theBeagle– a hard and wearisome journey, but geologically interesting.

FitzRoy piloted the [Blonde] to rescue crew of wreckedChallenger.

CD has received letters that were missing, and others; for ten months there will be none to or from him.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   [9–12 August] 1835
letters.summary:
Expresses envy for WDF’s life as a clergyman.

Outlines homeward voyage; tells of his hope of seeing active volcanoes and Tertiary strata in Galapagos. Recommends geology to Fox. Discusses Lyell’s views; CD has become "a zealous disciple".

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   12 [August] 1835
letters.summary:
Looks forward to seeing volcanoes in Galapagos Islands.

Has altered his views on Cordillera formations as a result of another trip. Discusses his theory of their origin and history.

letters.title: To H. S. Fox   15 August 1835
letters.summary: Sends some geological specimens. Describes his recent trips and findings on the geology of the Andes. Asks if HSF has seen large beds of shells on elevated land – possibly at Rio Grande or S. Brazil.

letters.title: To Alexander Burns Usborne[c. 1–5 September 1835]
letters.summary: Memorandum of geological instructions to guide ABU during a voyage of [Constitucion] to survey the coast of Peru.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   3 [September] 1835
letters.summary: Living quietly on the ship and eating good food has been good for him. He longs for home. Peru is in a miserable state.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   30 October 1835
letters.summary:
Erasmus has received CD’s journal and two boxes; six large boxes are at Plymouth. Had feared them lost in wreck ofChallenger.

News of family and friends.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   22 November 1835
letters.summary:
Some of CD’s letters were read at Geological Society in London. Professor Sedgwick says of CD, "doing admirably … collection above all praise … will have a great name among the Naturalists of Europe".

Erasmus has taken office of Clerk to a Government Commissioner. Other family news.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   27 December 1835
letters.summary:
At sea 25 days from Galapagos to Tahiti, where they stayed ten days. It was delightful. Then three weeks to New Zealand, where they will be for ten days.

Convinced of high merit of missionaries.

Dislikes Augustus Earle’s book.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   29 December [1835]
letters.summary:
CD’s fame is spreading: she quotes Henslow ["Letters to Professor Henslow" (1835),Collected papers1: 3–16], and a passage in theAthenæum.

Adds news of family and friends.

letters.title: From C. D. Douglas   5 January 1836
letters.summary: Reports in detail on the 20 Feb 1835 earthquake and on volcanic activity into December of 1835. Encloses a letter sent to him describing the earthquake.

letters.title: To Philip Parker King   [21 January 1836]
letters.summary: CD informs PPK of his impending arrival at Dunheved, Penrith; news of his journey thus far.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [28–9] January 1836
letters.summary:
His joy at prospect of journey’s end in eight months’ time.

Observations on Australia.

Reports on his collecting in Galapagos – its flora and very curious birds; its instructive geology.

Tahiti and good work of missionaries.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   28 January 1836
letters.summary: CD’s impressions of Sydney and of FitzRoy’s character and temperament.

letters.title: From Catherine Darwin   29 January 1836
letters.summary:
They have been reading about the wreck of theChallenger; much impressed by Capt. FitzRoy’s bravery.

The W. D. Foxes have a daughter. Family news.

letters.title: From Susan Darwin   12 February 1836
letters.summary: CD’s 27th birthday. News of family and friends. A niece, Mary Susan Parker, born 31 January.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   14 February 1836
letters.summary: All prefer Hobart Town and its society to Sydney. CD’s view on emigration to colonies. All on board are homesick.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   15 February 1836
letters.summary:
Finds the voyage tedious at present.

Expects that the different scientific societies will be of the greatest use to his work in London when he returns home.

Gives some impressions of Australia.

letters.title: From Caroline Darwin   28 March 1836
letters.summary: News of friends and family.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   29 April 1836
letters.summary:
Keeling Islands, his first coral lagoons; he has been occupied with subject of coral formation for six months.

Very busy at sea rewriting old geological notes. Has difficulties with writing.

FitzRoy has proposed joint account of the journey, combining CD’s journal with his own.

Looks forward with anxiety to Henslow’s reaction to the geological notes.

letters.title: To Catherine Darwin   3 June 1836
letters.summary:
Will call on Sir J. Herschel, then take short trip in the African desert.

Horrified at the publication of "the little book of extracts" from his letters to Henslow ["Letters to Professor Henslow" (1835),Collected papers1: 3–16].

letters.title: ToSouth African Christian Recorder   28 June 1836
letters.summary: A defence of the work of missionaries in the Pacific islands and Australia. [The letter was apparently written by RF with supporting evidence quoted from CD’s journal. The letter is signed by RF alone. A summary conclusion, as printed, is signed by both:] "On the whole, balancing all that we have heard, and all that we ourselves have seen concerning the missionaries in the Pacific, we are very much satisfied that they thoroughly deserve the warmest support, not only of individuals, but of the British Government."

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   9 July 1836
letters.summary: Asks JSH to propose him for Geological Society. His meeting with Sir John Herschel and Andrew Smith at Cape of Good Hope.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   18 July 1836
letters.summary:
In five days of geologising on St Helena, he found that the shells on high land had been mistakenly identified as seashells. They are land shells, but of species no longer living.

Can think of nothing but the return to England and his family.

letters.title: To Susan Darwin   4 August [1836]
letters.summary:
Beagleis again in Brazil because of need to check on "singular disagreements in the Longitudes".

Pleased by Sedgwick’s praise.

letters.title: From William Owen Sr   5 October [1836]
letters.summary: Welcomes CD home; urges him to come to Woodhouse.

letters.title: To Josiah Wedgwood II   [5 October 1836]
letters.summary: Happily home, he sends thanks to his "first Lord of the Admiralty". Will visit Maer in two or three weeks.

letters.title: To Robert FitzRoy   6 October [1836]
letters.summary: CD describes his happy home-coming. Finds his family and Shrewsbury unchanged.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   6 October [1836]
letters.summary: His joy at being home. Anxious to see JSH for advice on his geological specimens.

letters.title: From Robert FitzRoy   [19–]20 October [1836]
letters.summary:
Sends news of his movements sinceBeagleput in at Falmouth. His charts are safe and already being engraved.

Announces his engagement.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   24 October [1836]
letters.summary:
Last four days have been spent calling on naturalists. Geologists have been kind, but zoologists seem to think a number of undescribed creatures a nuisance.

Will send his belongings to Cambridge, but eventually his quarters must be London.

FitzRoy is to be married.

letters.title: To Charles Whitley   24 October [1836]
letters.summary:
Congratulates CW on his marriage. Waiting in London tillBeaglearrives in Woolwich.

Describes recent visit to Henslow in Cambridge.

At a loss to arrange specimens and observations.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [30–1 October 1836]
letters.summary: CD in London to meet with naturalists about his collections. Lyell and Owen are helpful, but no one else, except R. E. Grant, seems to want to examine his specimens.

letters.title: To J. S. Henslow   [1 November 1836]
letters.summary:
Alerts JSH to boxes of specimens and letter of 30 Oct on the way by wagon.

Thomas Bell has expressed interest in CD’s Crustacea and reptiles.

CD’s ignorance about his botanical specimens embarrasses him.

Asks whether JSH is disappointed with Galapagos plants.

letters.title: To W. D. Fox   6 November [1836]
letters.summary:
All his affairs are most prosperous. Has found many who will undertake description of animals; he will work at the geology. Lyell has been most friendly and kind.

CD has been proposed to the Geological Society.

letters.title: To Charles Wilkes   [7 November 1836]
letters.summary: Arranges to meet CW for conversation.

letters.title: To Caroline Darwin   [9 November 1836]
letters.summary:
His fossil bones are unpacked and some are great treasures. He has some geology to do: R. I. Murchison has lent him a map and asked him to look at a part of the country he has been describing.

Their only protection against having Harriet Martineau as sister-in-law is that she works Erasmus too hard.

letters.title: From J. M. Herbert   [19 November 1836]
